q: Haymitch Abernathy mentors two tributes from District 12 who must survive a televised battle in an arena. The hero wears a mockingjay pin and forms an alliance with Rue, a young girl from District 11. She volunteers to replace her sister Primrose. For 10 points, name this young-adult novel by Suzanne Collins.

This mystery writer created the Belgian detective Hercule Poirot and the elderly spinster Miss Marple. She wrote And Then There Were None and Murder on the Orient Express. For 10 points, name this British author.
This ancient Greek storyteller is credited with fables such as "The Tortoise and the Hare" and "The Boy Who Cried Wolf." Each fable ends with a moral. For 10 points, name this author.

Jacob and Wilhelm collected German folk tales such as "Hansel and Gretel," "Rapunzel," and "Snow White." Their collection was published in 1812. For 10 points, give the surname shared by these two brothers.

Perseus Jackson learns that he is the son of Poseidon and attends Camp Half-Blood. His friends include Annabeth and Grover. For 10 points, name this author of the Lightning Thief and the series Percy Jackson and the Olympians.

This author wrote I, Robot and the Foundation series. He formulated the Three Laws of Robotics, the first of which states that a robot may not injure a human being. For 10 points, name this science-fiction author.
Ged, a wizard from the island of Gont, releases a shadow while studying at Roke. This book, by Ursula K. Le Guin, begins the Earthsea series. For 10 points, name this fantasy novel.

Co-written with Alex Haley, this book follows a man's life from being a hustler to becoming a minister in the Nation of Islam. He later made a pilgrimage to Mecca and was assassinated in 1965. For 10 points, name this autobiography.

In this graphic novel, Jews are drawn as mice, Germans as cats, and Poles as pigs. The author interviews his father Vladek about surviving Auschwitz. For 10 points, name this Pulitzer Prize-winning work by Art Spiegelman.

Rorschach, Doctor Manhattan, and Ozymandias are among the retired superheroes in this graphic novel. Alan Moore wrote it and Dave Gibbons illustrated it. For 10 points, name this twelve-issue series, published by DC Comics.

This novel by William Goldman features Westley, who is known as the Dread Pirate Roberts. Inigo Montoya, the swordsman, says "Hello, my name is Inigo Montoya." For 10 points, name this fairy tale about Buttercup.
A small bear lives in Hundred Acre Wood with a donkey named Eeyore, a pig named Piglet, and a boy named Christopher Robin. He loves honey. For 10 points, name this character created by A. A. Milne.

A boy named Max is sent to bed without supper after misbehaving in a wolf suit. His bedroom turns into a forest, and he sails to an island where he becomes king of the creatures there, who roar their terrible roars. When he returns, his supper is still hot. For 10 points, name this picture book written and illustrated by Maurice Sendak.
This ancient Chinese military treatise attributed to Sun Tzu has thirteen chapters. It advises that the supreme excellence is to subdue the enemy without fighting. For 10 points, name this classic.
Answer these questions about children's fantasy.
parts: Which British author wrote Charlie and the Chocolate Factory and Matilda?
Which fantasy author wrote The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings?
Which Philip Pullman novel features Lyra Belacqua and her daemon Pantalaimon?

q: Answer these questions about science fiction.
parts: Which author wrote Fahrenheit 451?
Which author wrote The Time Machine and The War of the Worlds?
Which Jules Verne novel features Captain Nemo and the submarine Nautilus?

q: Answer these questions about poetic forms.
parts: Which Japanese form has three lines with five, seven, and five syllables?
Which fourteen-line form was used by Petrarch and Shakespeare?
Which poetic form of nineteen lines uses two refrains and was used by Dylan Thomas in "Do not go gentle into that good night"?

q: Answer these questions about Holocaust literature.
parts: Which girl wrote a diary in the Secret Annex?
Which Italian chemist wrote If This Is a Man, a memoir of Auschwitz?
Which Austrian psychiatrist wrote Man's Search for Meaning?

q: Answer these questions about picture books.
parts: Which author wrote The Cat in the Hat?
Which author wrote and illustrated The Very Hungry Caterpillar?
Which author wrote Goodnight Moon?

q: Answer these questions about mythology and folk tales.
parts: Which ancient Greek writer is credited with fables?
Which German brothers collected "Cinderella" and "Rumpelstiltskin"?
Which Roman writer's Metamorphoses retells Greek and Roman myths?

q: Answer these questions about mystery writers.
parts: Which British author created Hercule Poirot?
Which American author created the detective Sam Spade in The Maltese Falcon?
Which author created Lord Peter Wimsey?

q: Answer these questions about nonfiction narratives.
parts: Which diarist hid in Amsterdam during the Holocaust?
Which abolitionist wrote an autobiography about being enslaved in Maryland?
Which Henry David Thoreau essay argues for refusing to support an unjust government?

q: This hero was raised on the island of Seriphos after his mother Danae was set adrift in a chest. He used a mirrored shield from Athena and a curved sword from Hermes on a quest. He later rescued Andromeda from a sea monster. For 10 points, name this Greek hero who beheaded Medusa.

This monster had snakes for hair and turned anyone who met her gaze to stone. She was one of three Gorgon sisters but the only mortal one. Pegasus sprang from her blood after her beheading. For 10 points, name this monster killed by Perseus.

This musician charmed Charon and Cerberus with his lyre while searching the Underworld for his wife Eurydice. He was told not to look back until they reached the surface, but he did anyway. He was later torn apart by Maenads. For 10 points, name this Thracian poet.

This goddess was abducted by Hades while picking flowers. Her mother's grief caused the seasons to change when she had to spend part of each year below the earth after eating pomegranate seeds. For 10 points, name this daughter of Demeter and queen of the Underworld.

This Titan was punished by being chained to a rock where an eagle ate his liver every day. He had angered Zeus by stealing a gift from the gods for humans. For 10 points, name this Titan who gave humanity fire.

After Epimetheus accepted her as a wife, this woman opened a jar given by the gods. Out flew all the evils of the world, leaving only hope inside. She was created by Hephaestus at the order of Zeus. For 10 points, name this first woman in Hesiod's account.

This Athenian hero sailed to Crete with a group of youths and maidens as tribute. With help from Ariadne's thread, he found his way out of a maze after killing its inhabitant. His father Aegeus threw himself into the sea after he forgot to change his sails. For 10 points, name this slayer of the Minotaur.

This beast with the head of a bull and the body of a man lived at the center of a Labyrinth. It was the son of Pasiphae and a bull sent by Poseidon. For 10 points, name this creature slain by Theseus.

This hero was driven mad by Hera and killed his own family, so he performed penance by completing a series of labors for King Eurystheus. His tasks included capturing the Erymanthian boar and cleaning the Augean stables. For 10 points, name this son of Zeus and Alcmene, known as Hercules to the Romans.

This king of Ithaca came up with the idea of the Trojan Horse. After the war he spent ten years trying to get home, blinding the Cyclops Polyphemus on the way. His wife Penelope waited for him. For 10 points, name this hero of an epic by Homer.

This greatest Greek warrior at Troy was dipped in the River Styx by his mother Thetis. He sulked in his tent after a quarrel with Agamemnon over Briseis. He was killed by an arrow to his heel. For 10 points, name this hero of the Iliad.

This prince of Troy was the eldest son of Priam and the husband of Andromache. He killed Patroclus in battle and was then killed in a duel outside the city walls. His body was dragged behind a chariot. For 10 points, name this Trojan defender slain by Achilles.

This Trojan escaped his burning city carrying his father Anchises on his back. He later landed in Carthage, where he abandoned a queen who killed herself. For 10 points, name this son of Venus and the hero of Virgil's epic.

This goddess of wisdom and war sprang fully grown from the head of Zeus. Her symbols include the owl and the olive tree, and she won the contest to be patron of a city that took her name. For 10 points, name this goddess associated with the Parthenon.

This twin brother of Artemis drove the sun across the sky in later tradition. He was the god of music, prophecy, and healing, and was worshiped at Delphi. For 10 points, name this Greek god of the lyre.

This god of the sea carried a trident and caused earthquakes. He lost a contest with Athena over the patronage of Athens and was the father of Polyphemus. For 10 points, name this brother of Zeus and Hades, called Neptune by the Romans.

This messenger god wore winged sandals and carried a caduceus. He was the son of Zeus and Maia and was the guide of souls to the Underworld. For 10 points, name this god who was called Mercury in Rome.

This god of wine and revelry was born from the thigh of Zeus after his mother Semele died. He was accompanied by satyrs and Maenads and carried a staff topped with a pine cone called a thyrsus. For 10 points, name this god known as Bacchus in Rome.

This god of war was the son of Zeus and Hera and was disliked by many other gods. He was caught in a net by her husband Hephaestus while with his lover. For 10 points, name this Greek god whose Roman counterpart is Mars.

This goddess of love was said to have risen from the sea foam near Cyprus. She was married to Hephaestus but had an affair with Ares, and she was the mother of Eros. For 10 points, name this goddess called Venus by the Romans.

This son of Zeus was invited to dine with the gods but tested them by serving up his own son Pelops as a meal. His punishment in the Underworld was to stand in water beneath a fruit tree, with both the water and fruit receding whenever he reached for them. For 10 points, name this king whose name gives us an English verb meaning to tease.

This beautiful youth fell in love with his own reflection in a pool and wasted away. The nymph Echo had loved him in vain. A flower is named for him. For 10 points, name this figure from Ovid's Metamorphoses.

This swift huntress refused to marry any man who could not beat her in a footrace. Hippomenes won by dropping golden apples that she stopped to pick up. She also drew first blood in the Calydonian boar hunt. For 10 points, name this Greek heroine.

This craftsman built the Labyrinth for King Minos of Crete and also made a wooden cow for Pasiphae. Imprisoned by Minos, he escaped the island using wings made of feathers and wax, which cost the life of his son. For 10 points, name this legendary Athenian inventor.

This hero led the Argonauts on a quest for the Golden Fleece. He was aided by the sorceress Medea, whom he later abandoned for Glauce. For 10 points, name this Thessalian prince who sailed on the Argo.

This king of Thebes unknowingly killed his father Laius and married his mother Jocasta. He solved the riddle of the Sphinx and later blinded himself on learning the truth. For 10 points, name this tragic hero of a Sophocles play.

This king of Corinth was condemned to eternally push a boulder up a hill only to watch it roll down again. He had cheated death more than once. For 10 points, name this figure whose name describes a futile task.

This Titan was forced to hold up the sky on his shoulders as punishment after the war with the Olympians. The Hesperides were his daughters, and Heracles briefly took his place while he fetched golden apples. For 10 points, name this Titan, whose name is given to a book of maps.

This monstrous dog with three heads guarded the gates of the Underworld, fawning on those who entered but devouring any who tried to leave. The Roman poet Virgil says Aeneas drugged him with a honey cake, and Orpheus lulled him with music. Capturing him was the twelfth labor of Heracles. For 10 points, name this hound of Hades.

This daughter of Oedipus defied King Creon by burying her brother Polynices, who had been declared a traitor. Creon ordered her sealed in a cave, where she hanged herself. Her fiance Haemon killed himself after. For 10 points, name this title character of a Sophocles play.
Answer these questions about the twelve labors of Heracles.
parts: Heracles had to kill this many-headed water serpent that regrew heads when cut off.
This beast with an impenetrable pelt was strangled by Heracles, who then wore its skin.
Heracles had to retrieve the golden apples guarded by these nymphs, daughters of Atlas or Nyx.

q: Answer these questions about gods of the Greek pantheon.
parts: This king of the gods ruled from Mount Olympus and threw thunderbolts.
This craftsman god was thrown from Olympus and was married to Aphrodite.
This goddess of the hearth was one of the first Olympians and tended the sacred fire.

q: Answer these questions about the Trojan War.
parts: This Trojan prince's abduction of Helen set off the war.
This Greek king of Mycenae led the expedition and sacrificed his daughter Iphigenia.
This Trojan prophetess was cursed never to be believed by Apollo.

q: Answer these questions about the Underworld in Greek myth.
parts: This god ruled the Underworld.
This river had to be crossed by the dead on a ferry piloted by Charon, and oaths of the gods were sworn on it.
Souls who drank from this river forgot their past lives.

q: Answer these questions about monsters encountered by Greek heroes.
parts: These one-eyed giants forged thunderbolts for Zeus and were freed by him from Tartarus.
These bird-women lured sailors to their deaths with beautiful singing; Odysseus had his men plug their ears with wax.
This whirlpool, personified as a monster, lay opposite Scylla in a narrow strait.

q: Answer these questions about Greek women who were transformed.
parts: This weaver was turned into a spider by Athena after boasting about her skill.
This nymph was cursed to only repeat the last words spoken to her.
This girl, loved by Apollo, was turned into a laurel tree to escape him.

q: Answer these questions about Roman myth.
parts: This founder of Rome was raised by a she-wolf along with his twin brother.
This Roman god of war, counterpart of Ares, gives his name to a month.
This two-faced Roman god of beginnings gave his name to a month.

q: Answer these questions about the heroes who sailed with Jason.
parts: Jason sailed on this ship, named for its builder.
Jason sought this prize, hanging in a grove guarded by a dragon in Colchis.
This harpist was among the Argonauts and drowned out the Sirens with his music.

q: This god hung for nine nights on a tree and sacrificed an eye at Mimir's well in exchange for wisdom. He rides an eight-legged horse and carries the spear Gungnir. His ravens Huginn and Muninn bring him news. For 10 points, name this one-eyed chief of the Norse gods.

This god wields a hammer and rides a chariot pulled by two goats. He is the son of Odin and fights the giants, and thunder is said to be the sound of his chariot. For 10 points, name this Norse god of thunder.
This trickster god is the father of Fenrir and Hel and gave birth to the horse Sleipnir after turning into a mare. He arranged the death of Baldr. For 10 points, name this Norse shapeshifting god.

This god was killed by an arrow made of mistletoe, thrown by his blind brother Hodr at the urging of Loki. His death was mourned by all of creation except one giantess. For 10 points, name this beautiful son of Odin and Frigg.

This god of war put his hand in the mouth of the wolf Fenrir as a pledge and lost it when the wolf realized he was being tricked. He is associated with justice and single combat. For 10 points, name this one-handed Norse god.

This watchman of the gods lives at the end of the rainbow bridge and has such keen senses that he can hear grass grow. He will blow the horn Gjallarhorn at the start of the final battle. For 10 points, name this guardian god.

This wife of Odin was the goddess of marriage and foresight. She tried to make all things swear not to harm her son Baldr but overlooked the mistletoe. For 10 points, name this Norse queen of the gods.

This giant ash tree connects the nine worlds in Norse cosmology. An eagle sits at its top, a serpent gnaws at its roots, and a squirrel runs up and down it carrying insults. For 10 points, name this world tree.
In this hall in Asgard, Odin gathers warriors who died bravely in battle. They fight each day and feast each night. For 10 points, name this Norse afterlife hall whose name means hall of the slain.

In this prophesied battle, Surtr will set the world aflame, Odin will be swallowed by Fenrir, and Thor will die after killing the world serpent. Afterward, the world will rise again from the sea. For 10 points, name this Norse end of the world.

This giant wolf, a son of Loki, was raised among the gods, but only Tyr dared feed him. The gods bound him with the ribbon Gleipnir after he broke two other chains. He is fated to break free at Ragnarok and swallow Odin. For 10 points, name this monstrous wolf.

This sea serpent grew so large that it encircled the world and bit its own tail. Thor once tried to catch it while fishing and will fight it at Ragnarok. For 10 points, name this child of Loki, also called the Midgard Serpent.
The dwarves Brokkr and Sindri forged this weapon, which has a short handle because Loki interfered during its making. It always returns to its owner. For 10 points, name this weapon of Thor.

This ribbon, forged by dwarves, bound the wolf Fenrir after he broke other chains. It was made from six impossible things, including the sound of a cat's footfall, the beard of a woman, and the roots of a mountain. For 10 points, name this magical fetter.

This burning rainbow bridge connects Midgard to Asgard and is guarded by the watchman Heimdall. Thor must wade through rivers instead of crossing it, since his weight and fire would break it. For 10 points, name this bridge in Norse myth.
This realm is the home of the Aesir gods. It is surrounded by a wall built by a giant in exchange for the sun, the moon, and the goddess Freya. For 10 points, name this Norse city of the gods.

These female figures, whose name means choosers of the slain, ride into battle and bring the dead to Valhalla, where they serve mead to the warriors. Brynhild is a famous example of one. For 10 points, name these warrior maidens in the service of Odin.

This giantess rules the realm of the dishonored dead, where she is half living flesh and half corpse. She is the daughter of Loki and the giantess Angrboda. For 10 points, name this Norse goddess of the underworld.

This goddess guarded the apples that keep the gods young. She was kidnapped by the giant Thjazi after Loki, who had been threatened, tricked her into leaving Asgard. For 10 points, name this wife of the poet Bragi.

This god of the Vanir is the twin brother of Freya and the father of Freyr. He is the god of the sea and ships and was sent to live among the Aesir as a hostage. For 10 points, name this Norse sea god, who was married to Skadi.
This god of the Vanir owns the ship Skidbladnir and a sword that fights by itself, which he gave up to win the giantess Gerd. For 10 points, name this Norse god of fertility, the brother of Freya.

This goddess of love and beauty owns the necklace Brisingamen and drives a chariot pulled by cats. She is the sister of Freyr, and she receives half of those slain in battle in her hall Folkvangr. For 10 points, name this Norse goddess.

This primeval giant was killed by Odin and his brothers Vili and Ve, and the world was made from his body. His blood became the seas, his skull the sky, and his bones the mountains. For 10 points, name this first being in Norse myth.

This primeval cow licked the salty ice of Ginnungagap, freeing Buri, an ancestor of the gods. She fed the giant Ymir with her milk, and her name means something like hornless cow of the void. For 10 points, name this cow in Norse cosmology.

This severed head was consulted by Odin for advice. He was killed by the Vanir during an exchange of hostages and is known for his wisdom. For 10 points, name this guardian of a well of knowledge beneath Yggdrasil.

This dwarf-made ring, owned by Odin, drips eight new rings every ninth night. Odin placed it on the funeral pyre of his son Baldr, but Baldr returned it from Hel through Hermod. For 10 points, name this golden ring.
This hero killed the dragon Fafnir and bathed in its blood. He was later betrayed and killed by Gunnar's family, and his wife was Gudrun. For 10 points, name this hero of the Volsunga saga.

This squirrel runs up and down Yggdrasil carrying insults between an eagle at the top and a serpent at the roots. It stirs up strife between creatures of the tree. For 10 points, name this messenger squirrel.

This dragon gnaws at the roots of Yggdrasil along with many other serpents. It also chews on the corpses of oath-breakers and murderers in the realm of the dead. For 10 points, name this Norse dragon.

This fire giant will come from Muspelheim with a flaming sword to burn the world at Ragnarok. He is said to guard that southern realm of fire from the beginning of time. For 10 points, name this giant, whose name means black.
Answer these questions about Norse gods and their possessions.
parts: Odin's spear has this name.
Thor's wife is a goddess with golden hair, which Loki cut off as a prank.
This ship of Freyr can be folded up and kept in a pouch.

q: Answer these questions about Norse cosmology.
parts: This is the name of the world of humans.
This realm, home of the Vanir gods, is where Njord was born.
This realm of ice lies to the north and contains the well Hvergelmir.

q: Answer these questions about Norse figures in the story of Baldr.
parts: This god was killed by a mistletoe dart.
This blind god threw the fatal dart.
This giantess, possibly Loki in disguise, refused to weep for Baldr, so he stayed in Hel.

q: Answer these questions about the children of Loki.
parts: This wolf will swallow Odin at Ragnarok.
This eight-legged horse was Loki's offspring.
This serpent is thrown into the sea by Odin and grows to encircle Midgard.

q: Answer these questions about Norse beings other than gods.
parts: The three Norns tend the roots of this tree.
These craftsmen beings, such as Brokkr and Sindri, forged the treasures of the gods.
These beings were the lords of Alfheim, whose name literally means elves of light.

q: Answer these questions about the Norse gods of two clans.
parts: The clan of gods including Odin and Thor.
The clan including Njord, Freyr, and Freya, who joined the first group after a war.
These two ravens, whose names mean thought and memory, fly around the world each day.

q: Answer these questions about Sigurd and the Volsungs.
parts: Sigurd slew this dragon, who had been a dwarf.
This valkyrie slept on a mountain ringed with fire until Sigurd woke her.
This dwarf, Fafnir's brother, taught Sigurd the smith's art and urged him to kill the dragon.

q: Answer these questions about the story of Thor.
parts: Thor's hammer is called this.
This giant, king of Utgard, tricked Thor with illusions in a series of contests.
Thor and Loki visited this giant, who stole the hammer and demanded Freya's hand in marriage.

q: This god was said to sail across the sky in a solar barque each day and through the Underworld each night, where he fought the serpent Apep. He was often shown with the head of a falcon topped by a sun disk. For 10 points, name this Egyptian sun god.

This Egyptian god of the dead was murdered by his brother Set, and his body was cut into pieces. His wife Isis reassembled him, and he became ruler of the Underworld. For 10 points, name this green-skinned god, the father of Horus.

This goddess used her magic to gather the scattered pieces of her husband Osiris. She hid her son Horus in the marshes of the Nile Delta to protect him from Set. For 10 points, name this Egyptian goddess of magic and motherhood.

This lion-headed Egyptian goddess was sent by Ra to punish humanity for rebelling against him. She was stopped only when the gods tricked her into drinking beer dyed red to look like blood. For 10 points, name this goddess of war and healing.

This god of chaos, storms, and the desert killed his brother Osiris and fought a long contest with his nephew for the throne. He is often shown with an animal head of uncertain type. For 10 points, name this Egyptian god.
This falcon-headed sky god lost an eye in battle with Set, and that eye became a symbol of protection. Pharaohs were considered his living embodiment. For 10 points, name this son of Isis and Osiris.
This ibis-headed Egyptian god of writing and wisdom recorded the results when the hearts of the dead were weighed. He was also associated with the moon and with scribes. For 10 points, name this god.

This Sumerian king of Uruk befriended the wild man Enkidu and later traveled in search of immortality after his friend died. He met Utnapishtim, who survived a great flood. For 10 points, name this hero of an ancient Mesopotamian epic.

This primeval goddess of salt water was split in two by Marduk, and her body formed the heavens and the earth. She had taken a monstrous form to avenge her mate Apsu. For 10 points, name this Babylonian dragon of chaos.
This Babylonian god became king of the gods after defeating Tiamat. He was the patron deity of the city of Babylon and is the hero of the Enuma Elish. For 10 points, name this god.

This Sumerian goddess descended through seven gates to the Underworld, losing an item of clothing at each. Her sister Ereshkigal killed her, but she was revived. For 10 points, name this goddess of love and war, whom the Akkadians called Ishtar.

This feathered serpent god of the Aztecs was also a god of wind and learning. He was said to have created humans from bones and his own blood. For 10 points, name this god whose Maya counterpart is Kukulkan.

This Aztec god of war and the sun was born fully armed from his mother Coatlicue. He killed his sister Coyolxauhqui, and he is associated with the founding of Tenochtitlan. For 10 points, name this patron deity of the Mexica.
This Aztec god of the night sky, whose name means smoking mirror, was the rival of Quetzalcoatl. He is often shown with a missing foot, replaced by an obsidian mirror. For 10 points, name this god.

This Hindu god is the preserver of the universe and has appeared in ten avatars, including Rama and Krishna. He is often depicted resting on the serpent Shesha. For 10 points, name this member of the Trimurti.

This Hindu god of destruction and transformation is depicted with a third eye and a crescent moon in his hair. He performs the cosmic dance of the Nataraja. For 10 points, name this god whose consort is Parvati.

This elephant-headed Hindu god is the remover of obstacles and the patron of scribes. He is the son of Shiva and Parvati and rides a mouse. For 10 points, name this god whose broken tusk he used to write the Mahabharata.

This prince of Ayodhya was exiled for fourteen years. His wife Sita was kidnapped by the demon king Ravana, and he rescued her with the aid of an army of monkeys. For 10 points, name this hero of the Ramayana.

This Hindu warrior goddess rides a lion or a tiger and holds weapons in each of her many arms. She was created by the gods to kill the buffalo demon Mahishasura. Her festival is celebrated during Navaratri. For 10 points, name this goddess.
This Hindu avatar of Vishnu acts as the charioteer of Arjuna and speaks the Bhagavad Gita on the battlefield. As a child, he was known for stealing butter. For 10 points, name this blue-skinned god.

This Irish hero's real name was Setanta, but he got his new name after killing the smith's hound and offering to take its place. He single-handedly defended Ulster during the Cattle Raid of Cooley. For 10 points, name this warrior of the Ulster Cycle.
This Irish hero gained knowledge by burning his thumb on the Salmon of Knowledge. He led the Fianna and was the father of the poet Oisin. For 10 points, name this legendary warrior.

This Japanese goddess of the sun hid in a cave after her brother Susanoo's misbehavior, plunging the world into darkness. The other gods lured her out with a mirror and a dance. For 10 points, name this ancestor of the imperial family.
This Japanese storm god, the brother of Amaterasu, was exiled from heaven. He slew the eight-headed serpent Yamata no Orochi and found the sword Kusanagi in its tail. For 10 points, name this god.

This Chinese Monkey King studied under a Taoist master, gained a staff that could change size, and caused chaos in heaven. He later escorted the monk Xuanzang on a journey in the novel Journey to the West. For 10 points, name this trickster.
This Polynesian demigod used a magical fishhook to pull islands from the sea. He is also credited with slowing the sun and with stealing fire. For 10 points, name this Hawaiian and Maori hero.
This Hawaiian goddess of volcanoes and fire lives in the crater of Kilauea. She is known for her fiery temper and her feud with her sister Namaka. For 10 points, name this goddess.

This West African trickster takes the form of a spider and won all the world's stories from the sky god Nyame. For 10 points, name this folktale hero who traveled to the Caribbean with enslaved Africans.

In this Slavic folktale, a witch lives in a hut that stands on chicken legs. She flies in a mortar and steers with a pestle, and she is sometimes helpful, sometimes dangerous. For 10 points, name this figure of Russian folklore.

This creator god of the Inca rose from Lake Titicaca and fashioned the sun, the moon, and the stars. He made the first people from stone and later wandered the land disguised as a beggar. For 10 points, name this Andean deity.
Answer these questions about the Egyptian gods.
parts: This goddess with cow ears and a sun disk was the goddess of love, music, and joy.
This crocodile-headed god was a patron of the Nile and the Faiyum.
This serpent, the enemy of Ra, was defeated every night as the sun boat traveled through the Underworld.

q: Answer these questions about the Epic of Gilgamesh.
parts: Gilgamesh was king of this ancient city.
This immortal man told Gilgamesh the story of the great flood.
Gilgamesh and Enkidu killed this creature, sent by the goddess Ishtar after Gilgamesh rejected her.

q: Answer these questions about the Ramayana.
parts: This wife of Rama was kidnapped by a demon.
This brother of the demon king Ravana defected to Rama and was crowned king of Lanka after the war.
This brother of Rama accompanied him into exile and stayed beside him throughout.

q: Answer these questions about Hindu deities.
parts: This god is the creator of the universe in the Trimurti.
This goddess of wealth and fortune is the consort of Vishnu.
This fierce goddess with a garland of skulls is a form of the divine mother who destroys evil.

q: Answer these questions about Aztec and Maya myth.
parts: This Aztec capital was built on an island in a lake, where an eagle was seen perched on a cactus.
This is the sacred Maya text that tells of the hero twins who defeated the lords of Xibalba.
This Maya feathered serpent god is the counterpart of the Aztec Quetzalcoatl.

q: Answer these questions about Celtic myth.
parts: This Irish king of the Fianna was the leader of Finn's band of warriors, of which Oisin was a member.
This Irish warrior goddess of battle often appeared as a crow.
These supernatural people of Irish myth, the Tuatha De Danann, retreated into mounds and became these figures of folklore.

q: Answer these questions about creation myths around the world.
parts: In Chinese myth, this giant separated heaven from earth with an axe and became the world after dying.
This Chinese goddess molded the first humans from yellow clay and repaired the broken sky.
In Japanese myth, these two gods stirred the sea with a jeweled spear to make the first land.

q: This object was found in 1799 near a port in the Nile Delta by soldiers of Napoleon's army. It bears a decree issued in 196 BC in three scripts, including Greek and Demotic. Jean-Francois Champollion used it to decipher Egyptian hieroglyphs. For 10 points, name this slab of granodiorite now in the British Museum.

In 1215, rebellious barons forced King John of England to seal this document at Runnymede. Its clause 39 promised that no free man would be imprisoned except by lawful judgment of his peers. It is often cited as a foundation of constitutional limits on rulers. For 10 points, name this "Great Charter."

This man's best-known work, printed in Mainz in the 1450s, was a Bible with 42 lines per page. He combined a screw press with movable metal type cast in a hand mold. His workshop was financed by loans from Johann Fust. For 10 points, name this German printer.

This constructed language was published in 1887 in a booklet called the Unua Libro. Its creator, a Polish ophthalmologist, wanted it to be a neutral second language for everyone. Its name comes from its creator's pseudonym, Doktoro, meaning "one who hopes." For 10 points, name this most widely spoken constructed language.

This man lost his sight in a childhood accident in his father's leather workshop. At age 15 he adapted a military code called night writing, invented by Charles Barbier. The system he developed uses cells of six raised dots. For 10 points, name this Frenchman who created a reading system for the blind.

This inventor and painter was helped by Alfred Vail in refining his electromagnetic telegraph. In 1844 he sent the message "What hath God wrought" from the Capitol to Baltimore. His name is given to a code of dots and dashes. For 10 points, name this American.

This man's assistant Thomas Watson heard the first sentence spoken over his device: "Come here, I want to see you." He received a patent for his invention in 1876. He was born in Edinburgh and taught speech to deaf students in Boston. For 10 points, name this inventor of the telephone.

One of these two siblings made the first powered flight on December 17, 1903, lasting twelve seconds. They tested gliders and built a wind tunnel in their Dayton bicycle shop. Their craft was the Flyer, flown at Kitty Hawk. For 10 points, name these brothers, Orville and Wilbur.

Its original definition came from a French expedition that surveyed the arc from Dunkirk to Barcelona. It was meant to equal one ten-millionth of the distance from the equator to the North Pole through Paris. It is the base unit of length in the metric system. For 10 points, name this unit, about 39 inches long.

Originally, this man's temperature scale was inverted, with 100 as the freezing point of water and 0 as its boiling point. Carl Linnaeus helped reverse it after his death. He was an astronomer at Uppsala who also measured the shape of the Earth in Lapland. For 10 points, name this Swede who gives his name to a scale on which water freezes at zero.

On this scale, talc is rated 1 and gypsum is rated 2. Quartz is 7 and corundum is 9. A mineral that can scratch another has a higher number on it. For 10 points, name this scale of mineral hardness topped by diamond at 10.

Created by an Irish-born officer of the Royal Navy, this scale originally described the effect of wind on a sailing ship's canvas. Its levels run from 0, "calm," up to 12. Force 12 is a hurricane. For 10 points, name this scale of wind speed.

Developed in 1935 by a seismologist at the California Institute of Technology, this logarithmic scale measures earthquake size. Each whole-number step means ground motion ten times greater. It has largely been replaced by moment magnitude. For 10 points, name this scale named for Charles Richter.

Established by a bequest from a Hungarian-born newspaper publisher, this prize is administered by Columbia University. First awarded in 1917, its categories include journalism, letters, drama, and music. Winners get a certificate and a cash award. For 10 points, name this American prize that honors writers and journalists.

This system was devised in 1876 by a librarian at Amherst College. It divides knowledge into ten main classes, such as 500 for natural sciences and 800 for literature. Books on library shelves are arranged by its numbers. For 10 points, name this classification system created by Melvil Dewey.

This Swedish botanist's Systema Naturae first appeared in 1735. He standardized binomial nomenclature, giving each species a genus name and a species name. He called humans Homo sapiens. For 10 points, name this "father of taxonomy."

This man's first book, a speller with a blue cover, taught generations of American children to read. In 1828 he published a two-volume dictionary that simplified spellings such as "color" and "theater." He was a Connecticut-born lexicographer. For 10 points, name this author of An American Dictionary of the English Language.

A black basalt stele topped by a relief of the sun god Shamash records this ruler's laws. It was found at Susa in 1901 and is now in the Louvre. Its laws include "an eye for an eye" punishments. For 10 points, name this king of Babylon.

This alphabet is named for a Byzantine missionary, Saint Cyril, though his associate probably did not design it. It is used for writing Russian, Ukrainian, Bulgarian, and Serbian. Many of its letters, such as the one shaped like a backward N, derive from Greek. For 10 points, name this alphabet.

This man, who was not literate in English, invented a syllabary for his people's language around 1821. Each of its symbols stands for a syllable rather than a single sound. Within a few years, thousands of his people had learned to read and write. For 10 points, name this Cherokee silversmith.

The Polish Cipher Bureau first broke early versions of this device. At Bletchley Park, Alan Turing and others read its messages with help from electromechanical bombes. It scrambled letters using rotors, a plugboard, and a reflector. For 10 points, name this cipher machine used by Nazi Germany.

The notes to a paper translating a lecture by Luigi Menabrea include what is often called the first computer program. It was an algorithm to calculate Bernoulli numbers on Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine. The author was the only legitimate child of Lord Byron. For 10 points, name this woman, the Countess of Lovelace.

In 1989, this British scientist working at CERN proposed a system of linked hypertext documents. He wrote the first web browser and server in 1990. He later founded the World Wide Web Consortium. For 10 points, name this inventor of the World Wide Web.

Introduced by a papal bull in 1582, this system dropped ten days that October. It was designed to fix drift in the date of Easter that the Julian system caused. Under its rule, a century year is a leap year only if divisible by 400. For 10 points, name this calendar used worldwide, named for Pope Gregory XIII.

An international conference in Washington in 1884 chose this English town's observatory as the zero of longitude. The prime meridian passes through the Royal Observatory there. Mean time at this location gives its name to a world time standard. For 10 points, name this London borough on the Thames.

This Swedish chemist made a fortune from dynamite and other explosives. His will set aside money to honor achievements in physics, chemistry, medicine, literature, and peace. The first prizes were given in 1901. For 10 points, name this man who established an annual set of prizes.

In 1901, this Italian engineer received a signal sent from Cornwall at his station on Signal Hill in Newfoundland. The signal was the letter S in Morse code. He shared the 1909 Nobel Prize in Physics for work on wireless telegraphy. For 10 points, name this inventor of a radio system.

After graduating from Yale, this man built a machine at a Georgia plantation that separated cotton fibers from seeds. He patented it in 1794. Later he promoted the idea of interchangeable parts in making muskets for the government. For 10 points, name this American inventor of the cotton gin.

In 1913 at the Highland Park plant, this man's company introduced a moving assembly line. In 1914 he announced a wage of five dollars for an eight-hour day. His cheap Model T put millions of Americans on the road. For 10 points, name this founder of a Detroit car company.

This imaginary line mostly follows the 180th meridian, though it bends around island groups such as Fiji and Kiribati. A traveler crossing it heading west skips ahead one calendar day. It lies opposite the prime meridian. For 10 points, name this line where each new calendar day begins.

q: This thinker's works are mostly dialogues in which his teacher asks questions about virtue, justice, and knowledge. He founded a school in a grove near Athens around 387 BC that lasted for centuries. His most famous student was Aristotle. For 10 points, name this author of the Republic and Symposium.

This philosopher was born in Stagira and served as tutor to Alexander the Great. He founded the Lyceum, where he and his students walked while discussing ideas, earning them the name Peripatetics. He wrote on logic, biology, physics, ethics, and politics. For 10 points, name this student of Plato.

This philosopher founded a school in Athens called the Garden. He taught that pleasure is the highest good but defined it as freedom from bodily pain and mental disturbance. He argued that "death is nothing to us" because when we exist, death is not, and when death exists, we are not. For 10 points, name this Greek founder of a school of hedonism.

This thinker from Citium on Cyprus came to Athens, where he taught at a painted porch. He founded a school whose members taught that virtue is sufficient for happiness and that the universe is governed by divine reason. A shipwreck is said to have turned him toward philosophy, after which he studied with the Cynic Crates. For 10 points, name this founder of Stoicism, who shares a first name with a paradox-maker from Elea.

This philosopher from Ephesus held that fire is the basic element and that everything is in constant change. A quote attributed to him says that no one steps into the same river twice. He taught that the universe is governed by a rational principle and that opposites are in tension. For 10 points, name this "obscure" pre-Socratic philosopher.

This thinker from Elea wrote a poem in which a goddess describes the Way of Truth and the Way of Opinion. He argued that what exists cannot come into being or pass away and that change and plurality are illusions. His student Zeno devised paradoxes to defend his views. For 10 points, name this Eleatic philosopher of "being," who gave his name to a dialogue by Plato.

With his teacher Leucippus, this philosopher from Abdera proposed that reality consists of indivisible particles moving in empty space. He held that differences between objects come from the shape, size, and arrangement of these particles. He is called the "laughing philosopher." For 10 points, name this Greek atomist.

This man founded a religious and philosophical community at Croton and was said to have believed that the soul is reborn in different bodies. He taught that all things are numbers and that numerical ratios govern music. A theorem about the sides of a right triangle is named for him. For 10 points, name this Greek thinker.

This Milesian is often called the first Western philosopher. He said that all things come from water and is said to have predicted a solar eclipse. Plato reports a story that he fell into a well while gazing at the stars. For 10 points, name this first of the seven sages of Greece.

This pre-Socratic from Miletus was a student of Thales who held that the first principle of all things is the boundless, or apeiron. He is credited with drawing an early map of the world and with explaining cosmic order as a kind of justice between opposites. For 10 points, name this philosopher whose name follows the prefix "Anaxi-" and ends in "-mander."

This philosopher from Acragas claimed that all things are composed of fire, air, earth, and water, which are moved by two forces called Love and Strife. Legend says he died by leaping into the crater of Mount Etna. He wrote poems titled On Nature and Purifications. For 10 points, name this pre-Socratic who proposed four "roots" of matter.

This sophist from Abdera is remembered for the claim that "man is the measure of all things." He charged fees to teach rhetoric and virtue and is the title character of a Platonic dialogue. His relativism holds that things are for each person as they appear to that person. For 10 points, name this Greek sophist.

Called the "Second Sage" after Confucius, this Chinese philosopher argued that human nature is inherently good and that everyone has four moral "sprouts," including compassion. He said a person who sees a child about to fall into a well will naturally feel alarm. His sayings are collected in a book named for him. For 10 points, name this Confucian thinker.

This Chinese philosopher is the author of a book of stories and parables that includes a tale of a man who dreamed he was a butterfly and wondered whether the butterfly was dreaming it was the man. He championed spontaneity and the relativity of viewpoints. Along with Laozi, he is a foundational figure of Daoism. For 10 points, name this thinker.

This Stoic from Corduba wrote On the Shortness of Life and Letters to Lucilius. He was tutor and later adviser to a Roman emperor, who eventually ordered him to commit suicide in 65 AD. He argued that wise people should face death and misfortune with calm. For 10 points, name this Roman Stoic who tutored Nero.

This author of a series of private notes called the Meditations was the last of the Five Good Emperors of Rome. He wrote in Greek, reminding himself to accept fate and focus on his own character. He ruled from 161 to 180 and died campaigning on the Danube. For 10 points, name this Stoic emperor.

Born into slavery in Phrygia, this Stoic taught that some things are "up to us" while others are not. His lectures were recorded by his student Arrian in the Discourses and a short handbook, the Enchiridion. He taught in Nicopolis after being expelled from Rome. For 10 points, name this former slave and Stoic philosopher.

This thinker's pupil Porphyry compiled his lectures into six groups of nine treatises called the Enneads. He taught that all reality emanates from an ineffable first principle, and that the soul can return to it through contemplation. Intellect and Soul rank below that source. For 10 points, name this third-century founder of a Platonic school who wrote about "the One."

This philosopher is said to have traveled with Alexander the Great's army to India, where he encountered Indian ascetics. He taught that because we cannot know the true nature of things, we should suspend judgment and thereby achieve tranquility. A school of skepticism is named for him. For 10 points, name this founder of the oldest school of Greek skepticism from Elis.

This philosopher from Clazomenae introduced the concept of nous, or mind, as the force that orders the world. He taught that the sun is a fiery mass of metal and was prosecuted for impiety in Athens. Pericles was among his students and friends. For 10 points, name this pre-Socratic who was said to be the first philosopher to teach in Athens.

This ten-book dialogue is set at the Piraeus and has Socrates examine what justice is in a city and in a soul. It argues that the best city would be ruled by philosophers and divides the soul into reason, spirit, and appetite. Its censorship of poetry is a famous controversy. For 10 points, name this major work of Plato.

In this story, prisoners chained in an underground cavern see only shadows cast on a wall by a fire. One prisoner is freed and goes up into the light, finally seeing the sun, which represents the Form of the Good. When he returns, the others mock him. For 10 points, name this allegory from Book VII of Plato's Republic that illustrates education and knowledge.

This work is divided into ten books and discusses virtue as a mean between excess and deficiency, with courage lying between cowardice and rashness. Two books discuss friendship and its types. It argues that the highest human good is activity of the soul in accordance with virtue. For 10 points, name this ethical treatise by Aristotle.

In this dialogue, the title character is prosecuting his own father for murder when he meets Socrates outside the courthouse. Socrates asks whether the pious is loved by the gods because it is pious, or whether it is pious because it is loved by the gods. The conversation ends without a definition. For 10 points, name this Platonic dialogue that gave its name to a dilemma about morality and divine command.

In this work, a man tells the jury that he is a gadfly sent to sting the city of Athens. He says that "the unexamined life is not worth living" and explains that his inquiries began after the oracle at Delphi called someone wise. The accusers include Meletus. For 10 points, name this account of the defense speech of Socrates written by Plato.

The narrator in this dialogue tells Echecrates about the last day of Socrates, who is in prison awaiting execution. Socrates offers arguments for the immortality of the soul to Simmias and Cebes. The work ends with the drinking of hemlock. For 10 points, name this Platonic dialogue named for its narrator.
